claim: Mutations in LRRK2 confer susceptibility to mycobacterial infection.
source: However, several studies have established that mutations in LRRK2 confer susceptibility to mycobacterial infection, suggesting LRRK2 also controls immunity.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies establishing this relationship.

claim: Loss of LRRK2 in macrophages induces elevated basal levels of type I interferon (IFN) and interferon stimulated genes (ISGs).
source: We demonstrate that loss of LRRK2 in macrophages induces elevated basal levels of type I interferon (IFN) and interferon stimulated genes (ISGs) and causes blunted interferon responses to mycobacterial pathogens and cytosolic nucleic acid agonists.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including RNA-seq and RT-qPCR results shown in Figure 1.

claim: Loss of LRRK2 causes blunted interferon responses to mycobacterial pathogens and cytosolic nucleic acid agonists.
source: We demonstrate that loss of LRRK2 in macrophages induces elevated basal levels of type I interferon (IFN) and interferon stimulated genes (ISGs) and causes blunted interferon responses to mycobacterial pathogens and cytosolic nucleic acid agonists.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data including RNA-seq, RT-qPCR, and western blot analyses shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Altered innate immune gene expression in Lrrk2 knockout (KO) macrophages is driven by a combination of mitochondrial stresses, including oxidative stress from low levels of purine metabolites and DRP1-dependent mitochondrial fragmentation.
source: Altered innate immune gene expression in Lrrk2 knockout (KO) macrophages is driven by a combination of mitochondrial stresses, including oxidative stress from low levels of purine metabolites and DRP1-dependent mitochondrial fragmentation.
evidence: This is supported by multiple experimental approaches including metabolomics (Figure 7), DRP1 phosphorylation assays (Figure 4), and rescue experiments with antioxidants and DRP1 inhibitors.

claim: Mitochondrial defects in Lrrk2 KO macrophages promote mtDNA leakage into the cytosol and chronic cGAS engagement.
source: Together, these defects promote mtDNA leakage into the cytosol and chronic cGAS engagement.
evidence: This is supported by data showing increased cytosolic mtDNA (Figure 3E), rescue of phenotypes by cGAS deletion (Figure 3A), and mtDNA depletion experiments (Figure 3I).

claim: Lrrk2 KO mice can control Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) replication.
source: While Lrrk2 KO mice can control Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) replication, they have exacerbated inflammation and lower ISG expression in the lungs.
evidence: This is supported by CFU data showing no significant differences in bacterial burdens between Lrrk2 KO and control mice (Figure 8C).

claim: Lrrk2 KO mice have exacerbated inflammation during Mtb infection.
source: While Lrrk2 KO mice can control Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) replication, they have exacerbated inflammation and lower ISG expression in the lungs.
evidence: This is supported by histopathology data showing increased inflammatory nodules and neutrophil infiltration in Lrrk2 KO mice (Figure 8G-J).

claim: Lrrk2 KO mice have lower ISG expression in the lungs during Mtb infection.
source: While Lrrk2 KO mice can control Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) replication, they have exacerbated inflammation and lower ISG expression in the lungs.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data from lung homogenates showing reduced expression of ISGs like Mx1, Irf9, and Gbp8 (Figure 8F).

claim: Mutations in leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) are a major cause of familial and sporadic Parkinson's disease (PD).
source: Mutations in leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) are a major cause of familial and sporadic Parkinson's disease (PD), a neurodegenerative disease characterized by selective loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta region of the midbrain (Cookson, 2017; Kim and Alcalay, 2017; Martin et al., 2014; Schulz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Parkinson's disease is characterized by selective loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta region of the midbrain.
source: Mutations in leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) are a major cause of familial and sporadic Parkinson's disease (PD), a neurodegenerative disease characterized by selective loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta region of the midbrain (Cookson, 2017; Kim and Alcalay, 2017; Martin et al., 2014; Schulz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Parkinson's disease pathology, supported by citations.

claim: LRRK2 has been implicated in cytoskeletal dynamics.
source: Despite LRRK2 having been implicated in a variety of cellular processes, including cytoskeletal dynamics (Civiero et al., 2018; Kett et al., 2012; Pellegrini et al., 2017), vesicular trafficking (Herbst and Gutierrez, 2019; Sanna et al., 2012; Shi et al., 2017), calcium signaling (Bedford et al., 2016; Calì et al., 2014), and mitochondrial function (Ryan et al., 2015; Singh et al., 2019; Yue et al., 2015), its precise mechanistic contributions to triggering and/or exacerbating PD and other disease pathologies are not known.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LRRK2 has been implicated in vesicular trafficking.
source: Despite LRRK2 having been implicated in a variety of cellular processes, including cytoskeletal dynamics (Civiero et al., 2018; Kett et al., 2012; Pellegrini et al., 2017), vesicular trafficking (Herbst and Gutierrez, 2019; Sanna et al., 2012; Shi et al., 2017), calcium signaling (Bedford et al., 2016; Calì et al., 2014), and mitochondrial function (Ryan et al., 2015; Singh et al., 2019; Yue et al., 2015), its precise mechanistic contributions to triggering and/or exacerbating PD and other disease pathologies are not known.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LRRK2 has been implicated in calcium signaling.
source: Despite LRRK2 having been implicated in a variety of cellular processes, including cytoskeletal dynamics (Civiero et al., 2018; Kett et al., 2012; Pellegrini et al., 2017), vesicular trafficking (Herbst and Gutierrez, 2019; Sanna et al., 2012; Shi et al., 2017), calcium signaling (Bedford et al., 2016; Calì et al., 2014), and mitochondrial function (Ryan et al., 2015; Singh et al., 2019; Yue et al., 2015), its precise mechanistic contributions to triggering and/or exacerbating PD and other disease pathologies are not known.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LRRK2 has been implicated in mitochondrial function.
source: Despite LRRK2 having been implicated in a variety of cellular processes, including cytoskeletal dynamics (Civiero et al., 2018; Kett et al., 2012; Pellegrini et al., 2017), vesicular trafficking (Herbst and Gutierrez, 2019; Sanna et al., 2012; Shi et al., 2017), calcium signaling (Bedford et al., 2016; Calì et al., 2014), and mitochondrial function (Ryan et al., 2015; Singh et al., 2019; Yue et al., 2015), its precise mechanistic contributions to triggering and/or exacerbating PD and other disease pathologies are not known.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Dysregulation of mitochondrial homeostasis has emerged as a centrally important mechanism underlying PD pathogenesis and neuronal loss.
source: Of all the cellular pathways affected by LRRK2 mutations, dysregulation of mitochondrial homeostasis has emerged as a centrally important mechanism underlying PD pathogenesis and neuronal loss (Cowan et al., 2019; Panchal and Tiwari, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: PARK2 (Parkin), PINK1, and DJ1 all play crucial roles in mitochondrial quality control via mitophagy.
source: Indeed, other PD-associated genes, such as PARK2 (Parkin), PINK1, and DJ1, all play crucial roles in mitochondrial quality control via mitophagy.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of Parkinson's disease research.

claim: LRRK2 has been implicated in mitophagy directly through interactions with the mitochondrial outer membrane protein MIRO.
source: LRRK2 has been implicated in mitophagy directly through interactions with the mitochondrial outer membrane protein MIRO (Hsieh et al., 2016), and several lines of evidence support roles for LRRK2 in controlling mitochondrial network dynamics through interactions with the mitochondrial fission protein DRP1 (Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: LRRK2 controls mitochondrial network dynamics through interactions with the mitochondrial fission protein DRP1.
source: LRRK2 has been implicated in mitophagy directly through interactions with the mitochondrial outer membrane protein MIRO (Hsieh et al., 2016), and several lines of evidence support roles for LRRK2 in controlling mitochondrial network dynamics through interactions with the mitochondrial fission protein DRP1 (Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Fibroblasts and iPSC-derived neurons from PD patients harboring mutations in LRRK2 exhibit defects in mitochondrial network integrity.
source: Accordingly, a number of different cell types, including fibroblasts and iPSC-derived neurons from PD patients harboring mutations in LRRK2 exhibit defects in mitochondrial network integrity as well as increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) and oxidative stress (Sison et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Fibroblasts and iPSC-derived neurons from PD patients harboring mutations in LRRK2 exhibit increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) and oxidative stress.
source: Accordingly, a number of different cell types, including fibroblasts and iPSC-derived neurons from PD patients harboring mutations in LRRK2 exhibit defects in mitochondrial network integrity as well as increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) and oxidative stress (Sison et al., 2018; Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mutations in LRRK2 impair NF-κB signaling pathways in iPSC-derived neurons.
source: For example, mutations in LRRK2 impair NF-κB signaling pathways in iPSC-derived neurons and render rats prone to progressive neuroinflammation in response to peripheral innate immune triggers (López de Maturana et al., 2016), and chemical inhibition of LRRK2 attenuates inflammatory responses in microglia ex vivo (Moehle et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Mutations in LRRK2 render rats prone to progressive neuroinflammation in response to peripheral innate immune triggers.
source: For example, mutations in LRRK2 impair NF-κB signaling pathways in iPSC-derived neurons and render rats prone to progressive neuroinflammation in response to peripheral innate immune triggers (López de Maturana et al., 2016), and chemical inhibition of LRRK2 attenuates inflammatory responses in microglia ex vivo (Moehle et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Chemical inhibition of LRRK2 attenuates inflammatory responses in microglia ex vivo.
source: For example, mutations in LRRK2 impair NF-κB signaling pathways in iPSC-derived neurons and render rats prone to progressive neuroinflammation in response to peripheral innate immune triggers (López de Maturana et al., 2016), and chemical inhibition of LRRK2 attenuates inflammatory responses in microglia ex vivo (Moehle et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in LRRK2 are associated with susceptibility to mycobacterial infection.
source: Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in LRRK2 are associated with susceptibility to mycobacterial infection, inflammatory colitis (Umeno et al., 2011), and Crohn's disease (Van Limbergen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to genome-wide association studies.

claim: Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in LRRK2 are associated with inflammatory colitis.
source: Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in LRRK2 are associated with susceptibility to mycobacterial infection, inflammatory colitis (Umeno et al., 2011), and Crohn's disease (Van Limbergen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a genome-wide association study.

claim: Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in LRRK2 are associated with Crohn's disease.
source: Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in LRRK2 are associated with susceptibility to mycobacterial infection, inflammatory colitis (Umeno et al., 2011), and Crohn's disease (Van Limbergen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a genome-wide association study.

claim: LRRK2 is abundant in many immune cells including B cells, dendritic cells, monocytes, and macrophages.
source: Consistent with a role for LRRK2 in pathogen defense and autoimmunity, it is abundant in many immune cells (e.g. B cells, dendritic cells, monocytes, macrophages), and expression of LRRK2 is induced in human macrophages treated with IFN-γ (Gardet et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Expression of LRRK2 is induced in human macrophages treated with IFN-γ.
source: Consistent with a role for LRRK2 in pathogen defense and autoimmunity, it is abundant in many immune cells (e.g. B cells, dendritic cells, monocytes, macrophages), and expression of LRRK2 is induced in human macrophages treated with IFN-γ (Gardet et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Loss of LRRK2 reduces IL-1β secretion in response to Salmonella enterica infection in macrophages.
source: Loss of LRRK2 reduces IL-1β secretion in response to Salmonella enterica infection in macrophages (Liu et al., 2017) and enhances expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines in response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) infection at early time points of mouse infection (Härtlova et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Loss of LRRK2 enhances expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines in response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) infection at early time points of mouse infection.
source: Loss of LRRK2 reduces IL-1β secretion in response to Salmonella enterica infection in macrophages (Liu et al., 2017) and enhances expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines in response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) infection at early time points of mouse infection (Härtlova et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Mitochondrial stress and hyper-activation of DRP1 in Lrrk2 KO macrophages leads to the release of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA).
source: Specifically, we demonstrate that mitochondrial stress and hyper-activation of DRP1 in Lrrk2 KO macrophages leads to the release of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), chronic engagement of the cGAS-dependent DNA sensing pathway, and abnormally elevated basal levels of type I IFN and ISGs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased cytosolic mtDNA (Figure 3E), elevated DRP1 phosphorylation (Figure 4), and rescue experiments with DRP1 inhibition (Figure 4E-F).

claim: Mitochondrial stress and hyper-activation of DRP1 in Lrrk2 KO macrophages leads to chronic engagement of the cGAS-dependent DNA sensing pathway.
source: Specifically, we demonstrate that mitochondrial stress and hyper-activation of DRP1 in Lrrk2 KO macrophages leads to the release of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), chronic engagement of the cGAS-dependent DNA sensing pathway, and abnormally elevated basal levels of type I IFN and ISGs.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that cGAS deletion rescues the elevated basal ISG phenotype in Lrrk2 KO macrophages (Figure 3A).

claim: High basal levels of type I IFN in Lrrk2 KO macrophages reprogram them to be refractory to innate immune stimuli.
source: These high basal levels of type I IFN appear to completely reprogram Lrrk2 KO macrophages, rendering them refractory to a number of distinct innate immune stimuli, including infection with Mtb.
evidence: This is supported by data showing blunted responses to multiple stimuli including Mtb, ISD, poly(I:C), and DMXAA (Figures 1 and 2).

claim: Mtb-infected Lrrk2 KO mice did not exhibit significant differences in bacterial burdens compared to controls.
source: While Mtb-infected Lrrk2 KO mice did not exhibit significant differences in bacterial burdens compared to controls, we did observe exacerbated pathology and lower expression of ISGs in the lungs at early infection timepoints.
evidence: This is supported by CFU data from infected mice (Figure 8C).

claim: Mtb-infected Lrrk2 KO mice exhibit exacerbated pathology at early infection timepoints.
source: While Mtb-infected Lrrk2 KO mice did not exhibit significant differences in bacterial burdens compared to controls, we did observe exacerbated pathology and lower expression of ISGs in the lungs at early infection timepoints.
evidence: This is supported by histopathology data showing increased inflammatory nodules and neutrophil infiltration (Figure 8G-J).

claim: Hundreds of genes are expressed significantly higher in uninfected Lrrk2 KO macrophages compared to HET controls.
source: Surprisingly, we identified hundreds of genes whose expression was significantly higher in Lrrk2 KO macrophages (blue genes, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1A heatmap.

claim: Well-characterized ISGs including Mx1, Ifit1, Irf7, and Rsad2 are expressed several times higher in uninfected Lrrk2 KO macrophages.
source: Taking a closer look at the most affected genes (zoom-in, right), we noted that a number of well-characterized ISGs (e.g. Mx1, Ifit1, Irf7, Rsad2, etc.) were expressed several times higher in macrophages lackingLRRK2 (p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1A and confirmed by RT-qPCR in Figure 1E.

claim: 'Interferon signaling' and 'Activation of IRF by cytosolic PRRs' are the top enriched pathways in uninfected Lrrk2 KO vs. HET BMDMs.
source: Unbiased canonical pathway analysis confirmed a global upregulation of ISGs, identifying 'Interferon signaling' and 'Activation of IRF by cytosolic PRRs' as the top enriched pathways in uninfected Lrrk2 KO vs. HET BMDMs (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by IPA software analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Many ISGs that are elevated at baseline in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs fail to induce to the same levels following Mtb infection.
source: Curiously, many of the same ISGs whose expression was statistically higher at baseline in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs failed to induce to the same levels following Mtb infection (e.g. Ifit, Cmpk2, Gbp2, Rsad2; Figure 1C, orange genes, zoom-in, left).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1C and confirmed by RT-qPCR in Figure 1E.

claim: Loss of Lrrk2 has no effect on Tnfa expression despite the transcript being dramatically induced upon Mtb infection.
source: Importantly, blunted expression was not observed for all immune genes; for example, loss of Lrrk2 had no effect on the NFκB gene Tnfa despite the transcript being dramatically induced upon Mtb infection (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Expression of ApoE is reduced in uninfected Lrrk2 KO BMDMs.
source: Interestingly, expression of several non-ISG, non-immune genes was reduced in uninfected Lrrk2 KO BMDMs, including ApoE, which has been repeatedly linked to inflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases, and Ldhb, a critical metabolic gene involved in post-glycolytic energy production (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Expression of Ldhb is reduced in uninfected Lrrk2 KO BMDMs.
source: Interestingly, expression of several non-ISG, non-immune genes was reduced in uninfected Lrrk2 KO BMDMs, including ApoE, which has been repeatedly linked to inflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases, and Ldhb, a critical metabolic gene involved in post-glycolytic energy production (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Lrrk2 KO macrophages exhibit a significant defect in ISG expression 8 hr post-infection with Mycobacterium leprae.
source: We measured a significant defect in ISG expression 8 hr post-infection in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs and Lrrk2 KO RAW 264.7 macrophages compared to control cells (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Transfection of immunostimulatory dsDNA (ISD) induces blunted Ifnb expression in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs.
source: Transfection of immunostimulatory dsDNA (ISD), which is recognized by cGAS and stimulates the STING/TBK1/IRF3 axis, induced blunted Ifnb expression in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs (Figure 2B), Lrrk2 KO peritoneal macrophages (PEM) (significant differences in Ifnb expression were measured between Lrrk2 KO and HET at baseline but induction differences failed to reach statistical significance via 2-way ANOVA Tukey post-hoc testing) (Figure 2C), Lrrk2 KO RAW 264.7 macrophages (Figure 2D), Lrrk2 KO mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) (Figure 2E), and Lrrk2 KD RAW 264.7 macrophages (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2B-F.

claim: Lrrk2 KO BMDMs fail to fully induce Ifnb when stimulated with DMXAA.
source: We also found that Lrrk2 KO BMDMs failed to fully induce Ifnb if we bypassed cGAS and stimulated the DNA sensing adapter STING directly using the agonist DMXAA (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Lrrk2 KO macrophages show a significant defect in the ability to signal through IFNAR (phospho-STAT1).
source: In support of a defect in cytosolic nucleic acid sensing and IFNAR signaling, western blot analysis of IRF3 (phospho-Ser396) and STAT1 (phospho-Tyr701) activation showed a significant defect in the ability of Lrrk2 KO macrophages to signal through IFNAR (phospho-STAT1) and a modest defect in cytosolic DNA sensing (phospho-IRF3) over the course of 6 hr following ISD transfection (Figure 2H, quantitation below, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Lrrk2 KO macrophages show a modest defect in cytosolic DNA sensing (phospho-IRF3).
source: In support of a defect in cytosolic nucleic acid sensing and IFNAR signaling, western blot analysis of IRF3 (phospho-Ser396) and STAT1 (phospho-Tyr701) activation showed a significant defect in the ability of Lrrk2 KO macrophages to signal through IFNAR (phospho-STAT1) and a modest defect in cytosolic DNA sensing (phospho-IRF3) over the course of 6 hr following ISD transfection (Figure 2H, quantitation below, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Lrrk2 KO BMDMs are defective in ISG expression following recombinant bioactive IFN-β treatment.
source: Lrrk2 KO BMDMs were, however, defective in ISG expression following recombinant bioactive IFN-β treatment (which directly engages with IFNAR) (Figure 2J and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: Treatment with an IFN-β neutralizing antibody reduces basal levels of ISGs in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs.
source: Indeed, when HET and KO Lrrk2 BMDMs were treated with an IFN-β neutralizing antibody, there was a reduction in basal levels of Isg15 and Irf7 in Lrrk2 KO cells (Figure 2K and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Loss of IFNAR signaling reduces basal ISG levels in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs.
source: We next tested if loss of IFNAR signaling could similarly rescue the Lrrk2 KO phenotype by crossing Lrrk2 KO mice to Ifnar KO mice. In Lrrk2/Ifnar double KO BMDMs, we also observed a significant reduction in basal ISG levels (Figure 2L and Figure 2—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Loss of cGAS significantly reduces basal ISG expression in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs.
source: Although basal Isg15 expression differences between Lrrk2 KO and HET BMDMs were more modest in this experiment, loss of cGAS significantly reduced basal ISG expression in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: cGas/Lrrk2 double KO macrophages respond normally to DMXAA and poly(I:C) transfection.
source: With lowered resting type I IFN levels, cGas/Lrrk2 double KOs were able to respond normally to IFN/ISG-generating innate immune stimuli like DMXAA, which bypasses cGAS and stimulates STING directly (Diner et al., 2013), and poly(I:C) transfection (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Levels of STAT1 phosphorylation are restored in cGas/Lrrk2 double KO macrophages.
source: Consistent with the ability of cGas ablation to rescue Lrrk2 KO baseline and induction defects, western blot analysis showed that levels of STAT1 phosphorylation were restored in cGas/Lrrk2 double KOs (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Lrrk2 KO MEFs have a more fragmented mitochondrial network, especially around the cell periphery.
source: As previously described for cells overexpressing wild-type or mutant alleles of LRRK2 (Yang et al., 2014), Lrrk2 KO MEFs had a more fragmented mitochondrial network, especially around the cell periphery, as evidenced by punctate TOM20 staining (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Lrrk2 KD RAW 264.7 macrophages have ~3 fold more cytosolic mtDNA compared to controls.
source: We found that although Lrrk2 KD cells had only slightly higher total mtDNA compared to controls (Figure 3D), they had ~3 fold more cytosolic mtDNA (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: TFAM and VDAC are not detectable in the cytosolic fraction of Lrrk2 KD cells by western blot.
source: This increase in cytosolic mtDNA was not simply an artifact of fragmented mitochondria contaminating cytosolic fractions as neither TFAM, an abundant mitochondrial transcription factor, nor VDAC, a mitochondrial outer membrane protein, were detectable in the cytosolic fraction by western blot (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Depleting TFAM in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs leads to even higher basal ISG expression.
source: To exacerbate the proposed mitochondrial defect, we crossed Lrrk2 KO mice with Tfam HET mice. Tfam HET mice are deficient in the mitochondrial transcription factor required for maintaining the mtDNA network and thus have high levels of cytosolic mtDNA (Kasashima et al., 2011; West et al., 2015). Depleting TFAM in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs led to even higher basal ISG expression (Figure 3G), further suggesting that release of mtDNA into the cytosol in Lrrk2 KO cells contributes to their elevated type I IFN expression.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Treating Lrrk2 KO RAW 264.7 cells with ddC substantially reduces mtDNA copy number.
source: We next sought to rescue type I IFN defects in Lrrk2 KO macrophages by depleting mtDNA using ddC (2',3'-dideoxycytidine), an inhibitor of mtDNA synthesis (Leibowitz, 1971; Meyer and Simpson, 1969). Treating Lrrk2 KO RAW 264.7 cells with ddC substantially reduced mtDNA copy number (Figure 3H) and resulted in similar basal expression of type I IFN and ISGs in resting Lrrk2 HET and KO cells (Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: mtDNA depletion with ddC restores the ability of Lrrk2 KO macrophages to induce Ifnb in response to ISD.
source: Importantly, when mtDNA-depleted Lrrk2 KO RAW 264.7 macrophages were stimulated with ISD, their ability to induce Ifnb was restored to that of wild-type; Lrrk2 KO macrophages induced Ifnb approximately 500-fold in the absence of ddC but approximately 5000-fold following ddC treatment while WT macrophages induced Ifnb between 4000–5000-fold +/- ddC treatment (Figure 3I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-E).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Lrrk2 KD RAW 264.7 cells have significantly higher levels of phospho-S616 DRP1 compared to controls.
source: Because DRP1 is known to be positively regulated via phosphorylation at Ser616 (Taguchi et al., 2007), we performed flow cytometry with an antibody specific for phospho-S616 DRP1 and observed significantly higher levels of phospho-S616 DRP1 in Lrrk2 KD RAW 264.7 cells, Lrrk2 KO BMDMs, and Lrrk2 KO MEFs compared to controls (Figure 4A,C,D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A, C, and D.

claim: DRP1 inhibition with Mdivi-1 returns ISG expression to control levels in Lrrk2 KD RAW 264.7 macrophages and Lrrk2 KO BMDMs.
source: Next, to test if DRP1 activity was linked to high basal type I IFN/ISG expression in Lrrk2 deficient cells, we chemically inhibited DRP1 with Mdivi-1 and measured basal gene expression levels. In Lrrk2 KD RAW 264.7 macrophages and Lrrk2 KO BMDMs, DRP1 inhibition returned ISG expression to control levels (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: DRP1 inhibition restores cytosolic mtDNA levels to those of control cells in Lrrk2 KD RAW 264.7 cells and Lrrk2 KO MEFs.
source: DRP1 inhibition also restored the cytosolic mtDNA levels in Lrrk2 KD RAW 264.7 cells and Lrrk2 KO MEFs to those of control cells (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Lrrk2 KO BMDMs have lower mitochondrial membrane potential compared to control cells.
source: Flow cytometry analysis of resting Lrrk2 HET and KO cells revealed lower levels of JC-1 dye aggregation (i.e., lower mitochondrial membrane potential) in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs (Figure 5A–B), Lrrk2 KD RAW 264.7 macrophages (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), and primary Lrrk2 KO MEFs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), compared to control cells.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data using JC-1 dye shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Lrrk2 KO BMDMs are more sensitive to mitochondrial damaging agents rotenone/ATP and FCCP.
source: In addition, Lrrk2 KO BMDMs were more sensitive to the mitochondrial damaging and depolarizing agents, rotenone/ATP and FCCP, as measured by both JC-1 (Figure 5C; RAW 264.7 Lrrk2 KDs and Lrrk2 KO MEFs in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B, respectively) and TMRE (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Treatment with Mdivi-1 normalizes mitochondrial membrane potential in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs.
source: Interestingly, the mitochondrial membrane potential of Lrrk2 KO BMDMs was normalized after treatment with Mdivi-1 to inhibit DRP1 (Figure 5E–F), suggesting that misregulation of DRP1 occurs upstream of LRRK2-dependent defects in mitochondrial membrane potential.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: Treatment with mitoTEMPO dramatically rescues basal ISG expression in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs.
source: To test whether ROS could contribute to the defective type I IFN signature in Lrrk2 KO cells, we treated Lrrk2 HET and KO BMDMs with mitoTEMPO (mitoT), a mitochondrially-targeted scavenger of superoxide (Liang et al., 2010). Consistent with oxidative stress driving misregulation of the type I IFN response in the absence of LRRK2, we observed a dramatic rescue of basal ISG expression in Lrrk2 KO cells treated with mitoT (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Addition of sodium pyruvate to growth media increases basal levels of type I IFN in macrophages and MEFs lacking LRRK2.
source: Remarkably, addition of as little as 1 mM sodium pyruvate to the growth media increased the already high basal levels of type I IFN in macrophages and MEFs lacking LRRK2 (Figure 6A–B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that increasing metabolic demands on mitochondria promotes further leakage of mtDNA into the cytosol in these cells.
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Mitochondria in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs are defective in both maximal and reserve respiratory capacity.
source: We found that mitochondria in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs were defective in both maximal and reserve respiratory capacity (Figure 6C, top panels), indicating reduced OXPHOS.
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse metabolic analyzer data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Lrrk2 KO macrophages have reduced glycolysis.
source: Lrrk2 KO macrophages were also defective in non-glycolytic acidification and had reduced glycolysis. (Figure 6C, bottom panels).
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse metabolic analyzer data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Co-treatment of Lrrk2 KO BMDMs with mitoT and IFN-β neutralizing antibody completely restores OXPHOS and glycolysis.
source: Remarkably, co-treatment of Lrrk2 KO BMDMs with mitoT and IFN-β neutralizing antibody completely restored OXPHOS and glycolysis. This rescue was greater than treatment of either IFN-β blockade or mitoT alone (Figure 6C–D), indicating that mitochondrial ROS and constitutive IFNAR signaling independently contribute to the metabolic defects in Lrrk2 KO macrophages.
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse metabolic analyzer data shown in Figure 6C-D.

claim: Lrrk2 KO BMDMs have lower levels of inosine monophosphate (IMP) and hypoxanthine.
source: In Lrrk2 KO BMDMs, we found lower levels of inosine monophosphate (IMP) and hypoxanthine, two intermediates in the purine biosynthesis pathway, which we validated using pure molecular weight standards (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: This is supported by LC/MS/MS data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Lrrk2 KO MEFs have significantly fewer de novo biosynthesis puncta containing FGAMS per cell compared to HET controls.
source: Moreover, in accordance with lower levels of purine metabolites, we observed significantly fewer de novo biosynthesis puncta containing formylglycinamidine ribonucleotide synthase (FGAMS, also known as PFAS), a core purinosome component, per Lrrk2 KO MEF cell compared to HET controls (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 7C-D.

claim: Addition of urate reduces basal ISG expression in a dose-dependent fashion in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs and Lrrk2 KD RAW 264.7 cells.
source: To test this, we first supplemented cells with antioxidants in order to rescue the type I IFN defect in Lrrk2 KO macrophages. Addition of urate, a free radical scavenger and major breakdown product of purine metabolism (Figure 7B), reduced basal ISG expression in a dose-dependent fashion in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs and in Lrrk2 KD RAW 264.7 cells (Figure 7E–F, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 7E-F.

claim: Treatment with urate or mitoT restores the resting mitochondrial membrane potential of Lrrk2 KO BMDMs.
source: Furthermore, treatment with urate or mitoT restored the resting mitochondrial membrane potential of Lrrk2 KO BMDMs (Figure 7G–H), suggesting that radical oxygen species contribute to mitochondrial depolarization in the absence of LRRK2.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7G-H.

claim: Neither urate nor mitoT is sufficient to alter DRP1 activation in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs.
source: Neither urate nor mitoT was sufficient to alter DRP1 activation in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs, suggesting the antioxidant defects are either downstream or independent of LRRK2-dependent DRP1 misregulation (Figure 7I).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 7I.

claim: There is a significant increase in CFUs recovered from Lrrk2 KO BMDMs at 5 days following Mtb infection.
source: Lrrk2 HET and KO BMDMs were infected with Mtb (Erdman strain; MOI = 1), and colony forming units (CFUs) were measured over the course of five days. We observed a significant increase in CFUs recovered at 5 days (120 hr) following infection (Figure 8A), suggesting that while Lrrk2 KO macrophages can control Mtb replication early after infection, they are more permissive once the bacteria have established a niche.
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: There is no difference in survival time of Mtb-infected Lrrk2 KO mice compared to HET controls.
source: We observed no difference in the survival time of Mtb-infected Lrrk2 KO mice compared to HET controls (Figure 8B), and at Days 7, 21, 63, and 126 days post-infection, we observed no significant differences in bacterial burdens in the lungs or spleens of infected mice (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: There are no significant differences in bacterial burdens in the lungs or spleens of Mtb-infected Lrrk2 KO and HET mice at Days 7, 21, 63, and 126 post-infection.
source: We observed no difference in the survival time of Mtb-infected Lrrk2 KO mice compared to HET controls (Figure 8B), and at Days 7, 21, 63, and 126 days post-infection, we observed no significant differences in bacterial burdens in the lungs or spleens of infected mice (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by CFU data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Major NF-κB pathway inflammatory cytokines (Tnfa, Il6, Il1b) are expressed at similar levels in the lungs of Mtb-infected Lrrk2 KO and HET mice at Day 21.
source: While major NF-κB pathway inflammatory cytokines (e.g. Tnfa, Il6, Il1b) were expressed at similar levels in the lungs of Mtb-infected Lrrk2 KO and HET mice at Day 21 (Figure 8E), we observed lower levels of several canonical ISGs including Mx1, Irf9, and Gbp8 (Figure 8F), consistent with trends we observed in Lrrk2 KO macrophages ex vivo (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data from lung homogenates shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Lower levels of ISGs including Mx1, Irf9, and Gbp8 are observed in the lungs of Mtb-infected Lrrk2 KO mice at Day 21.
source: While major NF-κB pathway inflammatory cytokines (e.g. Tnfa, Il6, Il1b) were expressed at similar levels in the lungs of Mtb-infected Lrrk2 KO and HET mice at Day 21 (Figure 8E), we observed lower levels of several canonical ISGs including Mx1, Irf9, and Gbp8 (Figure 8F), consistent with trends we observed in Lrrk2 KO macrophages ex vivo (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data from lung homogenates shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Significantly more inflammatory granulomatous nodules are observed in the lungs of Lrrk2 KO mice at Day 21 post-Mtb infection, specifically in the perivascular region.
source: We observed significantly more inflammatory granulomatous nodules in the lungs, specifically in the perivascular region (Figure 8G–H), indicating that more macrophages had infiltrated infected lungs of Lrrk2 KO mice at Day 21 post-infection.
evidence: This is supported by histopathology data shown in Figure 8G-H.

claim: More total neutrophils and more degenerate neutrophils are observed in the lungs of Mtb-infected Lrrk2 KO mice compared to controls.
source: Consistent with increased inflammation, we observed more total neutrophils (polymorphonuclear leukocytes, PMNs) as well as more PMNs undergoing cell death (degenerate PMNs) in the lungs of Mtb-infected Lrrk2 KO mice compared to controls (Figure 8I–J).
evidence: This is supported by histopathology data shown in Figure 8I-J.

claim: 4 hr is a key innate immune time point during Mtb infection, corresponding to the peak of transcriptional activation downstream of several pattern recognition receptors.
source: Previous studies have identified 4 hr as a key innate immune time point during Mtb infection, corresponding to the peak of transcriptional activation downstream of several pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), including the cytosolic DNA sensor cGAS (Manzanillo et al., 2012; Watson et al., 2015; Watson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mycobacterium leprae shares a virulence-associated ESX-1 secretion system with Mtb.
source: We began by infecting macrophages with Mycobacterium leprae (Mlep), which shares a virulence-associated ESX-1 secretion system with Mtb and also induces type I IFN through cytosolic nucleic acid sensing (de Toledo-Pinto et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about M. leprae, supported by a citation.

claim: Mycobacterium leprae induces type I IFN through cytosolic nucleic acid sensing.
source: We began by infecting macrophages with Mycobacterium leprae (Mlep), which shares a virulence-associated ESX-1 secretion system with Mtb and also induces type I IFN through cytosolic nucleic acid sensing (de Toledo-Pinto et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: ISD is recognized by cGAS and stimulates the STING/TBK1/IRF3 axis.
source: Transfection of immunostimulatory dsDNA (ISD), which is recognized by cGAS and stimulates the STING/TBK1/IRF3 axis, induced blunted Ifnb expression in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs (Figure 2B), Lrrk2 KO peritoneal macrophages (PEM) (significant differences in Ifnb expression were measured between Lrrk2 KO and HET at baseline but induction differences failed to reach statistical significance via 2-way ANOVA Tukey post-hoc testing) (Figure 2C), Lrrk2 KO RAW 264.7 macrophages (Figure 2D), Lrrk2 KO mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) (Figure 2E), and Lrrk2 KD RAW 264.7 macrophages (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the mechanism of ISD action.

claim: DMXAA bypasses cGAS and stimulates STING directly.
source: With lowered resting type I IFN levels, cGas/Lrrk2 double KOs were able to respond normally to IFN/ISG-generating innate immune stimuli like DMXAA, which bypasses cGAS and stimulates STING directly (Diner et al., 2013), and poly(I:C) transfection (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Mtb is a potent activator of type I IFN expression through perturbation of the Mtb-containing phagosome and release of bacterial dsDNA into the cytosol.
source: Mtb is a potent activator of type I IFN expression, thought to occur mostly through perturbation of the Mtb-containing phagosome and release of bacterial dsDNA into the cytosol, where it is detected by DNA sensors like cGAS, activating the STING/TBK1/IRF3 axis (Collins et al., 2015; Wassermann et al., 2015; Watson et al., 2015; Wiens and Ernst, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) is a potent activator of type I IFNs downstream of cGAS.
source: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) has been shown to be a potent activator of type I IFNs downstream of cGAS (West et al., 2015), and LRRK2 is known to influence mitochondrial homeostasis (Singh et al., 2019), albeit through mechanisms that are not entirely clear.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Tfam HET mice have high levels of cytosolic mtDNA.
source: To exacerbate the proposed mitochondrial defect, we crossed Lrrk2 KO mice with Tfam HET mice. Tfam HET mice are deficient in the mitochondrial transcription factor required for maintaining the mtDNA network and thus have high levels of cytosolic mtDNA (Kasashima et al., 2011; West et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: ddC (2',3'-dideoxycytidine) is an inhibitor of mtDNA synthesis.
source: We next sought to rescue type I IFN defects in Lrrk2 KO macrophages by depleting mtDNA using ddC (2',3'-dideoxycytidine), an inhibitor of mtDNA synthesis (Leibowitz, 1971; Meyer and Simpson, 1969).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LRRK2 contributes to mitochondrial homeostasis through interaction with the mitochondrial fission protein DRP1 in microglia.
source: Previous studies of microglia have shown that LRRK2 contributes to mitochondrial homeostasis through interaction with the mitochondrial fission protein DRP1 (Ho et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: DRP1 is positively regulated via phosphorylation at Ser616.
source: Because DRP1 is known to be positively regulated via phosphorylation at Ser616 (Taguchi et al., 2007), we performed flow cytometry with an antibody specific for phospho-S616 DRP1 and observed significantly higher levels of phospho-S616 DRP1 in Lrrk2 KD RAW 264.7 cells, Lrrk2 KO BMDMs, and Lrrk2 KO MEFs compared to controls (Figure 4A,C,D).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Macrophages typically switch from OXPHOS to glycolysis when activated.
source: This result was surprising as macrophages typically switch from OXPHOS to glycolysis when activated (Kelly and O'Neill, 2015), but Lrrk2 KO macrophages have reduced utilization of both energy producing pathways.
evidence: This is established knowledge in immunometabolism, supported by a citation.

claim: Purine metabolism is tightly associated with generation of antioxidant compounds.
source: Interestingly, purine metabolism is tightly associated with generation of antioxidant compounds, and several metabolites in this pathway are well-characterized biomarkers of Parkinson's disease (Figure 7B; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Several metabolites in the purine metabolism pathway are well-characterized biomarkers of Parkinson's disease.
source: Interestingly, purine metabolism is tightly associated with generation of antioxidant compounds, and several metabolites in this pathway are well-characterized biomarkers of Parkinson's disease (Figure 7B; Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Urate is a free radical scavenger and major breakdown product of purine metabolism.
source: Addition of urate, a free radical scavenger and major breakdown product of purine metabolism (Figure 7B), reduced basal ISG expression in a dose-dependent fashion in Lrrk2 KO BMDMs and in Lrrk2 KD RAW 264.7 cells (Figure 7E–F, respectively).
evidence: This is established knowledge about urate's biochemical properties.

claim: LRRK2 missense mutations are associated with exacerbated inflammation and poor disease outcomes in leprosy patients.
source: These data help explain why LRRK2 missense mutations are associated with exacerbated inflammation and poor disease outcomes in leprosy patients (Fava et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Type I IFNs are important biomarkers of Mtb infection associated with poor outcomes in humans and in mouse models of infection.
source: Mtb is a potent activator of cytosolic DNA sensing (Manzanillo et al., 2012; Watson et al., 2012), and type I IFNs are important biomarkers of Mtb infection associated with poor outcomes in humans and in mouse models of infection (Berry et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: IFNAR signaling is required for nitric oxide production in macrophages ex vivo.
source: New insights into the requirement of IFNAR signaling for nitric oxide production in macrophages ex vivo suggest critical roles for type I IFN induction in cell-intrinsic control of Mtb replication (Banks et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: Loss of cGAS almost completely abrogates type I IFN expression in macrophages.
source: Our previous experiments demonstrated that while loss of cGAS almost completely abrogates type I IFN expression in macrophages, it has only minor effects in vivo (serum IFN-β levels and lung type I IFN/ISG expression levels) (Collins et al., 2015; Watson et al., 2015), suggesting that Mtb infection can elicit type I IFN expression in important cGAS-independent ways in vivo that we do not yet fully understand.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: Loss of cGAS has only minor effects on type I IFN expression in vivo during Mtb infection.
source: Our previous experiments demonstrated that while loss of cGAS almost completely abrogates type I IFN expression in macrophages, it has only minor effects in vivo (serum IFN-β levels and lung type I IFN/ISG expression levels) (Collins et al., 2015; Watson et al., 2015), suggesting that Mtb infection can elicit type I IFN expression in important cGAS-independent ways in vivo that we do not yet fully understand.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies by the authors.

claim: A recent publication reported a significant decrease in CFUs in Lrrk2 KO mice at very early infection time points (Day 7 and 14) during Mtb infection.
source: Another recent publication that investigated the role of LRRK2 in controlling Mtb infection does report a significant decrease in CFUs in Lrrk2 KO mice at very early infection time points (Day 7 and 14), which correlates with increased inflammation in the lungs (as we also report) (Härtlova et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: LRRK2 inhibitors are a major area of drug development for the treatment of PD.
source: Because LRRK2 inhibitors are a major area of drug development for the treatment of PD, it is crucial to understand how both loss of and mutations in this protein might impact the ability of patients receiving such therapies to respond to and clear infection.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of Parkinson's disease therapeutics.

claim: The plasma of PD patients contains significantly less hypoxanthine and uric acid.
source: Lower levels of purine nucleotide intermediates are especially notable in the context of PD; the plasma of PD patients (both LRRK2 mutant-associated and idiopathic) has been shown to contain significantly less hypoxanthine and uric acid (Johansen et al., 2009), and patients with higher plasma urate levels, despite carrying LRRK2 mutations, are less likely to develop PD (Bakshi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Patients with higher plasma urate levels, despite carrying LRRK2 mutations, are less likely to develop PD.
source: Lower levels of purine nucleotide intermediates are especially notable in the context of PD; the plasma of PD patients (both LRRK2 mutant-associated and idiopathic) has been shown to contain significantly less hypoxanthine and uric acid (Johansen et al., 2009), and patients with higher plasma urate levels, despite carrying LRRK2 mutations, are less likely to develop PD (Bakshi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Urate is currently being investigated as a potential therapeutic of PD.
source: Furthermore, urate is currently being investigated as a potential therapeutic of PD, highlighting the importance of purine biosynthesis in this disease.
evidence: This is established knowledge about current PD therapeutic research.

claim: Overexpression of both wild type LRRK2 and the PD-associated G2019S allele of LRRK2 causes mitochondrial fragmentation.
source: Previous reports have shown that LRRK2 can physically interact with DRP1 and that LRRK2 mediates mitochondrial fragmentation through DRP1 (Wang et al., 2012). Overexpression of both wild type LRRK2 and the PD-associated G2019S allele of LRRK2 have been shown to cause mitochondrial fragmentation (Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: LRRK2 kinase activity has been linked to DRP1 activation via phosphorylation at T595 in neurons.
source: Previous studies have linked LRRK2 and LRRK2 kinase activity to DRP1 activation via phosphorylation at several sites including T595 in neurons (Su and Qi, 2013) and S616 in a neuron-like carcinoma cell line (Esteves et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: LRRK2 kinase activity has been linked to DRP1 activation via phosphorylation at S616 in a neuron-like carcinoma cell line.
source: Previous studies have linked LRRK2 and LRRK2 kinase activity to DRP1 activation via phosphorylation at several sites including T595 in neurons (Su and Qi, 2013) and S616 in a neuron-like carcinoma cell line (Esteves et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Other kinases including ERK2 and CDK1 can phosphorylate DRP1 at S616.
source: Indeed, other kinases have been shown to phosphorylate DRP1 at S616 in other cell types, including ERK2 (Kashatus et al., 2015) and CDK1 (Taguchi et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: shRNA knockdown of LRRK2 in HeLa cells inhibits purinosome assembly and disassembly.
source: A recent human kinome screen identified LRRK2 as a kinase involved in dynamics of the purinosome, a cellular body composed of purine biosynthetic enzymes that assembles at or on the mitochondrial network (French et al., 2016). Specifically, shRNA knockdown of LRRK2 in HeLa cells inhibited purinosome assembly and disassembly.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Purinosomes are posited to form in order to protect unstable intermediates and increase metabolic flux through the de novo purine biosynthetic pathway.
source: As purinosomes are posited to form in order to protect unstable intermediates and increase metabolic flux through the de novo purine biosynthetic pathway (An et al., 2008; Schendel et al., 1988), we propose that the lower levels of IMP and hypoxanthine we measure in Lrrk2 KO macrophages results from LRRK2-dependent defects in purinosome assembly (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Tonic or basal IFN levels are thought to 'rev the engine' so that cells can rapidly induce type I IFN expression after receiving a stimulus.
source: Typically, tonic or basal IFN levels are thought to 'rev the engine' so that cells can rapidly induce type I IFN expression after receiving a stimulus (Taniguchi and Takaoka, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge about type I IFN priming, supported by a citation.

claim: Defective IFNAR signaling in BMDMs leads to increased Mtb replication.
source: These results are consistent with a recent report demonstrating that defective IFNAR signaling in BMDMs leads to increased Mtb replication (Banks et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a recent study.

claim: LRRK2's role in maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis is critical for proper induction of type I IFN gene expression in macrophages.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that LRRK2's role in maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis is critical for proper induction of type I IFN gene expression in macrophages and for downstream inflammatory responses during in vivo infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: LRRK2's role in maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis is critical for downstream inflammatory responses during in vivo infection.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that LRRK2's role in maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis is critical for proper induction of type I IFN gene expression in macrophages and for downstream inflammatory responses during in vivo infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: LRRK2 may play a role in regulating the central nervous system immune milieu in PD patients via alteration of mitochondrial homeostasis in brain-resident glial cells.
source: They also hint at a previously unappreciated but potentially crucial role for LRRK2 in regulating the central nervous system immune milieu in PD patients (Patrick et al., 2019) via alteration of mitochondrial homeostasis in brain-resident glial cells.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the findings, supported by a citation.

claim: Cytosolic DNA and increased ROS may together generate oxidized cytosolic DNA that is resistant to the exonuclease TREX-1.
source: We propose that cytosolic DNA and increased ROS— which perhaps together generate oxidized cytosolic DNA that is resistant to the exonuclease TREX-1 (Gehrke et al., 2013)—drive this unique refractory phenotype in Lrrk2 KO macrophages.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the data and supported by a citation.

claim: The refractory phenotype in Lrrk2 KO macrophages could be driven by upregulation of one or more unidentified negative regulators of key signaling pathways.
source: Alternatively or additionally, this phenomenon could be driven via by upregulation of one or more unidentified negative regulators of these key signaling pathways.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the observed phenotype.

claim: Loss of LRRK2 could alter DRP1 phosphorylation indirectly through changing serine accessibility or protein-protein interactions.
source: We propose that loss of LRRK2 could alter DRP1 phosphorylation indirectly through changing serine accessibility or protein-protein interactions, or by modifying other pathways that control mitochondrial turnover or lysosome homeostasis.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal to explain the observed DRP1 phosphorylation phenotype.

claim: Loss of LRRK2 could alter DRP1 phosphorylation by modifying other pathways that control mitochondrial turnover or lysosome homeostasis.
source: We propose that loss of LRRK2 could alter DRP1 phosphorylation indirectly through changing serine accessibility or protein-protein interactions, or by modifying other pathways that control mitochondrial turnover or lysosome homeostasis.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal to explain the observed DRP1 phosphorylation phenotype.

claim: Mtb infection can elicit type I IFN expression in important cGAS-independent ways in vivo.
source: Our previous experiments demonstrated that while loss of cGAS almost completely abrogates type I IFN expression in macrophages, it has only minor effects in vivo (serum IFN-β levels and lung type I IFN/ISG expression levels) (Collins et al., 2015; Watson et al., 2015), suggesting that Mtb infection can elicit type I IFN expression in important cGAS-independent ways in vivo that we do not yet fully understand.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from previous experimental data cited.
